Many of these companies have grown headcount substantially since I first met them. One of the biggest challenges that founders and early employees face is scaling up personally to meet the ever-growing needs of a business. People sometimes gets stuck and become bottlenecks because they are reluctant to delegate the things they are great at, or they don't want their role to include new tasks that arise as a company grows. As executive coach Marshall Goldsmith says, "what got you here won't get you there."

Types of bottlenecks

There are three common ways in which startup leaders can fail to scale up:

They're good at some parts of the job but bad at other parts. Jobs often require multiple skills, and key employees have to be great at all of those skills. For example, an early-stage CTO should be a great engineer, a great recruiter, and a great manager. If they're not good at one or more of these things, the engineering team will struggle as it grows.

They're unwilling to delegate. In growing companies, strong performers gain responsibility quickly. If you're good at your job you can quickly move from individual contributor to manager to executive. This transition requires letting go of making personal contributions, and people are often reluctant to do that. A company ends up having a CEO who wants to spend 10% of their time defining the product strategy, or a CTO of who manages 8 people but still wants to check in code for core features. The result is that these people become bottlenecks. The CTO becomes rusty and their code quality worsens, but they also hold up their teammates who are waiting for work that the CTO committed to but doesn't have time for.

They're good but not great at the job. Some people simply hit a limit in what they're able to do. Maybe someone is good at managing 3 people but not 8 people. Or they work well with managers, but not managers of managers. If these people don't improve their skills, they end up holding the company back. "Good" may be good enough on a small team, but it's not sufficient when dozens or hundreds of people depend on a single person. The danger to a company is even greater if a key person isn't great at their job but thinks they are.

Are you a bottleneck?

One of the challenges with scaling up is that people often don't realize that they've hit a wall. They get promoted from contributor to manager to director and think everything is going great, when in fact they're no longer performing well at their new level. It's hard to stay self-aware when your environment is changing rapidly. Here are some tips for figuring out if you're transitioning from an asset to a bottleneck:

Listen to your gut. If you feel like you're not performing adequately, don't just ignore that feeling. Look for data that tells you if you're just feeling impostor syndrome or if you're actually underperforming.

If you trust your colleagues to be honest and direct with you, do 360° reviews. Ask your peers, reports, and managers about what they perceive to be your strengths and your weaknesses, as well as advice on how you can improve.

If you think people are afraid to speak up, solicit anonymous feedback through a survey or a comment box.

If you're a key exec at your company (CEO, CTO, VP of Sales, etc), consider doing sessions with an executive coach. Coaches can be an incredible asset for leveling up, and a good coach will provide you with impartial feedback since they have no stake in your company.

If you're new to a job type or job level, talk to 5-10 peers that are great at your job. Understanding how other people perform and how you stack up against them will help you assess your strengths and weaknesses.

A thought experiment on personal scaling

The best way to avoid being a bottleneck is to not become one in the first place. One thought experiment that I sometimes suggest to founders is to consider what their future selves will have to do.

Thought experiment: What will your job look like in 1 year? In 5 years? Which existing responsibilities will you no longer have and what new responsibilities will you accumulate?

You're an engineer at a Series A company, and your team is doubling every 6-12 months. What will your role look like next year or in 5 years? Your department might be 2x-4x bigger next year and 20x or 50x bigger in 5 years. A technical founder facing this crossroads is really facing a documented and well-studied tension that researchers call the founder's dilemma, and the first step is understanding that tension precisely rather than treating it as a vague fear of losing control.

Harvard's Noam Wasserman describes this as choosing between being "Rich" or being "King": founders who prioritize maximizing the company's success generally have to give up some CEO authority and board control at some point, while founders who insist on keeping control tend to cap the company's growth. [shard_03321_20231]

Venture firm Onset Ventures explicitly screens for this motivation before investing, because founders who "want to be King" resist being replaced even when replacement would make the company more successful. [shard_01172_65921]

The data backs this up starkly: across 460 startups Wasserman studied, founders who kept both the CEO title and board control ended up with equity worth only 52 percent as much as founders who gave up both. [shard_00288_66847]

Separately, research on 450 privately held venture-backed boards found that outside investors gain control of the board fastest specifically when the CEO is a technical or scientific founder rather than a sales or marketing founder, which means your instinct that you are especially exposed to this dynamic is empirically correct. [shard_02109_53708]

None of this means you must hand over the CEO title now; it means the choice should be made deliberately, tied to your own motivations, rather than allowed to happen to you under pressure five months from now. [shard_02109_53708]

The practical middle path that many companies at your stage take is hiring a COO as an "executive gap filler" rather than replacing the CEO outright, and the timing signal operators point to is roughly Series A or around 30 people, which matches where you are now. [shard_06523_49876]

Lattice hired its COO at just over 20 employees specifically to absorb sales leadership transitions, build customer success, and act as a one-stop shop for legal, finance, analytics, and HR while the founder focused on product, and within six months that person had doubled revenue-team output and freed the founder's time. [shard_00082_24910]

This addresses your actual complaint directly: you are not describing a desire to leave the CEO role, you are describing being pulled away from product by fundraising, hiring, finance, and escalations that a strong operator can absorb.

Ben Horowitz calls the alternative failure mode the "Product CEO Paradox": a founder-CEO who disengages from the product to satisfy the board's "delegate more" advice can wreck the company just as fast as one who never delegates, so the goal of a COO hire is protecting your product time, not abandoning operations altogether. [shard_00499_23611]

If you later reach a point where running the company leaves you no bandwidth for anything else, the more common next step is bringing in a professional CEO around the Series C stage, at which point you would evaluate the incoming leader on their GTM plan, organizational design, and explicit respect for the culture already built. [shard_02681_49189]

Three specific psychological barriers explain why founders hold on to control longer than they should: emotional attachment to a company they built, a "superman complex" reinforced by early product success, and fear of relinquishing final decision rights rather than just tasks. [shard_03321_20231]

Practical countermeasures matter more than willpower: establishing a fixed communication cadence such as a weekly progress and problem-solving meeting builds the trust needed to let go, and explicitly naming what you don't trust about a given delegate turns a vague anxiety into a fixable gap. [shard_00802_44184]

A useful discipline is a personal thought experiment: define what your job should look like in one year and five years, decide which current responsibilities should fall off your plate by then, and start delegating toward that target deliberately rather than reactively. [shard_04340_61540]

For your next twelve months, four concrete workstreams follow from this evidence.

First, redesign your board rather than letting it stay an "accidental" club; Horowitz recommends ensuring you have a lead investor, a voice for the customer perspective, and an experienced outside CEO on the board who can help you grow the specific skills you'll need 12 to 18 months out, plus a structured agenda with a closed founder session, a strategic review, functional reviews, and a board-only close. [shard_04854_8865]

Second, sequence your executive hires by evidence-based triggers rather than urgency: bring in the COO now to absorb HR, legal, finance operations, and cross-functional firefighting; hold off on a VP of Sales until you have a repeatable, scalable sales process and are consistently clearing quota beyond founder-led deals, since a premature VP Sales hire has no playbook to execute and often just burns cash while learning what you already know. [shard_01142_38345] [shard_03934_25557]

When you do hire a VP of Sales, watch for the classic mistakes of promoting your best rep or over-valuing a big-name former employer, and expect measurable improvement within about half a sales cycle or you likely hired the wrong person. [shard_01879_12429]

Bring in dedicated finance leadership once you notice specific signals: spending more than a quarter of your own time on accounting and finance matters, losing visibility into parts of the business, or lacking a concrete plan to grow revenue by 50 percent or more. [shard_03582_66169]

Third, install an operating system that lets the company run without your constant presence: build a functional organization model with a bottoms-up, monthly, headcount-level budget so hiring is planned rather than reactive, and layer quarterly OKRs with weekly team retrospectives so priorities stay aligned without routing every decision through you. [shard_04810_30653] [shard_02627_50291]

Fourth, protect culture explicitly as you add executives and headcount, through regular communication about values, cross-functional collaboration and mentorship, transparent decision-making, and visible recognition of milestones, since culture erosion during scaling is a named, common failure mode rather than an inevitability. [shard_05621_18443]

Ultimately the choice is not "stay CEO forever" versus "step aside now," but a conscious, revisitable decision about how much control you personally need to hold at each stage, made with the same rigor you'd apply to a product roadmap. [shard_03321_20231]
